newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Sao Paulo sewage firm looks abroad for investments.
newsitem.headline: Sao Paulo sewage firm looks abroad for investments.

text.p: Sao Paulo state's sewage company Sabesp is looking abroad for partnerships to finance part of its ambitious $5.0 billion investment plan by the year 2000.

The search for foreign investment begins Thursday, when Sabesp president Ariovaldo Carmignani will be in Washington D.C. for meetings with officials from the World Bank and the InterAmerican Development Bank (IDB).

Sabesp or Companhia de Saneamento Basico do Estado de Sao Paulo is seeking some $1.3 billion from these two international loan bodies for projects to expand the state's sewage and water services, Carmignani told Reuters in an interview.

"We are moving to achieve the goal of reaching the end of this government supplying 100 percent of the (Sao Paulo) population with treated and piped water, serving 85 percent with sewage collection and having 60 percent of this sewage treated," said Carmignani.

Currently, Sabesp, which operates concessions granted by Sao Paulo's municipalities, provides water and sewage services for 22 million people, nearly 60 percent of Sao Paulo state's population, in 329 municipalities.
It supplies drinking water for 92 percent of the population and sewage collection for 68 percent and treats 26 percent of the sewage collected.

After Washington, Carmignani heads for London, where he meets foreign investors on Sept 17 for the launch of $30 million to $40 million in six-month Eurocommercial papers, the company's first attempt to raise money on international markets.

The funds raised will be earmarked for Sabesp's $5.0 billion investment program, of which $2.7 billion will be financed with the firm's own resources, while around $650 million are expected to come from private investors, Carmignani said.

Sabesp is also working with the World Bank's International Finance Corporation (IFC) on a public tender for a 202 million real project which will allow it to expand by 4,700 litres of water per second its capacity to provide water to the Sao Paulo area.
"The IFC is our advisor," said Carmignani, adding he expects tender details on the Juquia-Juquitiba project to be out in January or February and the contract to be awarded six months later.
The project will follow the Building, Operation and Transfer (BOT) model, under which private investors will build and operate the system while Sabesp will distribute the water.
The Sabesp chief said some ten other projects will be offered to private investors under the BOT model.

Carmignani will be travelling abroad Thursday with Sabesp's positive 1995 results in his briefcase. The firm, which showed an operational loss of $214 million in 1994, reported a net profit of $26 million last year, with revenues of $2.1 billion.
In the first half of 1996, the company's net profit totalled $231 million and its revenues reached $1.1 billion due to deep staffing cuts and a hike in revenues after a company restructuring.
